definition: The notion by which Danièle Hervieu-Léger defines religion in La Religion pour mémoire (1993): an ideological, practical and symbolic apparatus through which the consciousness, individual and collective, of belonging to a believing lineage is constituted, maintained, developed and controlled. To believe religiously is to believe in the name of a chain, drawing one's authority from a tradition that goes back to founding witnesses and that one takes on the task of passing on. Modernity is amnesiac: it breaks the chains of memory, and what fades away with the practising believer is religion as a shared self-evidence, Berger's canopy. Two figures take its place: the pilgrim, who composes his own itinerary, and the convert, who chooses his lineage. The essay notes that the convert touches on the criterion, that there are replacement lineages, the Nation, the Revolution, Onfray's Civilization, and that a spirituality without a lineage escapes refoundation but is not passed on: the modern pilgrim has no lineage; he has a library. See also Sacred canopy, Invisible religion, Secularization.

The central notion of Religion Explained (2001), by Pascal Boyer. The human mind has intuitive inference systems about persons, animals, objects and artefacts; a religious concept violates one expectation of one of these categories while respecting all the others: a spirit that has no body but sees, hears and remembers, a statue that listens to prayers, a dead ancestor who gets angry. These minimally counterintuitive concepts are better remembered than ordinary concepts, because they surprise, and better than concepts that are too bizarre, because they remain usable: one can reason about a jealous god. Religion is thus a by-product of faculties that have other functions, neither an adaptation nor a need: science is as unnatural as religion is natural. The essay takes from it that Boyer adds no regime to critique but explains why gods are easy to think, and that he refutes the idea of an empty place of exactly the shape of God; it objects that he explains beliefs, not exercises. See also Need and disposition, Animism, Projection.

Existential security, the variable that Pippa Norris and Ronald Inglehart place at the centre of Sacred and Secular (2004): the religiosity of a population depends on the degree to which its members feel protected against illness, poverty, violence and chance. Where existence is secure, in Scandinavia, practice and belief recede over several generations; where it is not, they persist, and the United States is explained by its inequalities rather than by a competitive religious market, against Rodney Stark. Since religious populations have more children, the world nonetheless has more believers than before: this is the demographic paradox. The essay uses these measurements as an empirical arbiter in the debate on the causes of belief: Lucretius, Hume, Freud and Becker, for whom fear is the source, are proved right; the Enlightenment, which expected secularization from critique, is proved wrong, for it is not critique that secularizes, it is health insurance; and Malinowski is confirmed, for whom belief recedes with uncertainty, not with knowledge. Exits from religion therefore presuppose a security that only institutions guarantee. See also Need and disposition, Secularization, Illusion.

The three conditions that William James lays down in “The Will to Believe” (1896) for it to be legitimate to believe without sufficient evidence. An option is living when both hypotheses are really possible for the one who chooses; forced when there is no third way and abstaining amounts to choosing; momentous when the stake is unique and irreversible. When an option is of this kind and reason cannot decide, our passional nature not only may but must decide, at our own risk, and James objects to Clifford, for whom believing without evidence is always a fault, that the fear of error is itself a passion: dupery for dupery, what proof is there that dupery through hope is so much worse than dupery through fear? The essay stresses the inner tolerance of this position, which defends faith without asking it of the unbeliever, and combines it with Clifford: one has the right to believe where reason leaves the question open, and this right ends where the belief engages the lives of others without their having chosen it. See also Ethics of belief, Pascal's wager, Reformed epistemology.

The current of analytic philosophy of religion whose principal figure is Alvin Plantinga. Against Clifford's evidentialism, which demands evidence for every belief, Plantinga observes that this principle does not satisfy its own conditions, being neither self-evident nor demonstrated, and maintains that belief in God can be properly basic, like belief in the existence of other minds: rational without being inferred. He finds its source in a theme of Calvin, the sensus divinitatis, a faculty or cognitive mechanism that produces belief in God in us in certain circumstances. The classic objection is that of the Great Pumpkin: if belief in God is basic without evidence, why not any belief whatever? Plantinga replies that certain candidate beliefs can be ruled out without having a general criterion. The essay judges that this debate, Plantinga's as well as the one Mackie opens on evil, saves the coherence and rationality of faith at the price of its universality: the believer can be rational, but can no longer demand that the unbeliever be rational by believing; and Ivan remains. See also Ethics of belief, Living, forced, momentous option, Fideism.

Cause of itself. The name metaphysics gives to God when it thinks of him as the ultimate ground of beings: Descartes uses it to say that God draws his existence from his own essence, Spinoza makes it the first definition of the Ethics, before relating it to substance. Heidegger, in the lecture on the onto-theological constitution of metaphysics (Identity and Difference, 1957), sees in it the proper name of the God of the philosophers and shows that such a god has nothing divine about it: to this god man can neither pray nor offer sacrifice; before the causa sui he can neither fall to his knees in awe nor play music and dance. Godless thinking, which must abandon the God of the philosophers, is perhaps closer to the divine god. Marion takes up the analysis to define the conceptual idol, a site, metaphysics, a function, theology in onto-theo-logy, a definition, the causa sui, then turns Heidegger against himself. Becker uses the expression in another sense: the causa sui project is man's effort to be his own cause and to deny death. See also Onto-theology, God of the philosophers, Idol and icon.

Unendlicher qualitativer Unterschied, the expression that Karl Barth takes over, in German, from Kierkegaard and places at the centre of his Epistle to the Romans (1919, recast in 1922). Against the liberal theology of the nineteenth century, which had made religion an expression of human consciousness, of feeling or of culture, Barth proclaims that God is in heaven and man on earth, and that nothing leads from one to the other, neither experience, nor history, nor morality: revelation alone crosses the abyss, from above to below. Barth writes in the preface to the second edition that if he has a system, it consists in keeping in view what Kierkegaard called the infinite qualitative difference between time and eternity. Barth concludes in § 17 of the Church Dogmatics (1938) that religion, the affair of godless man, is unbelief, and he had acknowledged as early as 1927 that Feuerbach is right all along the line about religion as human experience. It is the exact inverse of Stirner: the pious man is godless. Bonhoeffer will reproach this position with a positivism of revelation. See also Fideism, Religionless Christianity, Projection.

The programme Dietrich Bonhoeffer sketches in his prison letters of 1944, though the essay has not been able to verify the exact phrase religionsloses Christentum. On 30 April, he announces a completely religionless time, religion being for him metaphysics and inwardness, the stopgap God, Lückenbüßer, who is called upon at the limits of knowledge and power. On 16 July, he takes up Grotius's formula, etsi deus non daretur, as if God were not given: God as a working hypothesis has been abolished, and it is Feuerbach he names; before God and with God we live without God, and God is powerless and weak in the world. On 18 July, the world come of age, mündig gewordene Welt, is closer to God than the world not yet of age. Bonhoeffer distances himself from Barth, whom he reproaches with a positivism of revelation, a block of dogmas to take or leave, and from Bultmann, liberal at bottom. The essay sees in it the reversal of Feuerbach, Marx and Nietzsche: a weak God is no longer a projection but a dispossession. Bonhoeffer remains within revelation. See also Infinite qualitative difference, Projection, Demythologization.

The metaphysical heart of Simone Weil's thought, in the fragments Gustave Thibon gathered under the title Gravity and Grace (1947). To decreate is to make something created pass into the uncreated; to destroy is to make it pass into nothingness, a guilty substitute for decreation. Creation is an act of love by which God renounces being everything so that something may exist outside him; the creature must respond with a symmetrical renunciation, renounce being something, consent to be nothing so that God may be through it. This is why Weil can write that of two atheisms one is a purification of the notion of God, and can pray while thinking that God does not exist. The essay compares decreation with Eckhart's detachment and with Murdoch's unselfing, which transposes it into a soberer vocabulary. It sees in Weil the principal believing candidate for the rank of exception: a faith that refuses consolation, one must not have consolation, accepts affliction without justifying it and gives no meaning to suffering, which partly answers the Nietzschean objection of the ascetic ideal. See also Gelassenheit, Unselfing, Ascetic ideal.

The title of the first volume of Georges Bataille's Somme athéologique (1943), followed by Guilty (1944) and On Nietzsche (1945). In it Bataille describes a voyage to the end of the possible of man: a naked experience, detached from every confession, every Church and every salvation, which borrows from the mystics their states, ecstasy, anguish, rapture, while withdrawing their object. Its term is not God but non-knowledge, the night in which the subject loses himself; it is sovereign, that is, without any end other than itself, and it is bound up with expenditure, laughter, eroticism and sacrifice. Sartre replies in 1943, in “Un nouveau mystique” (“A New Mystic”), that Bataille has kept the corpse of God. The essay holds Bataille to be a key witness of the regime of experience, not an exception: the Somme refounds a sacred of transgression and confirms Durkheim, whom Bataille read through Acéphale. It sets Bataille's expenditure against Simone Weil's decreation; Bataille had known Weil and put her into a novel in the figure of Lazare. Onfray will take up the word atheology in an opposite sense. See also Atheology, The sacred, Eight regimes of critique.

In Camus's The Myth of Sisyphus (1942), the confrontation between the human call for meaning and the unreasonable silence of the world. The absurd lies in their encounter, and the question it raises is that of suicide. Camus rejects two ways out: suicide, which abolishes one of the terms, and the leap, which abolishes the other by giving the world a meaning it does not have; this is the reproach he addresses to Kierkegaard and Jaspers, guilty of philosophical suicide, the absurd becoming god. What remains is revolt, which maintains the tension and draws from it a rule of life: one must imagine Sisyphus happy. The essay reads in this formula a spirituality without consolation, and in The Rebel (1951) the passage from solitary absurdity to a revolt that discovers a we. The word has an older history in the series: James counts the feeling of the absurd among the trials of sick souls, and where Camus spoke of the absurd, Wittgenstein refuses even the name. The essay judges Camus's objection to Jaspers sound in logic, but not in the light of the criterion, for Jaspers's leap ends in no obedience. See also Revolt, Thought of noon, Philosophical faith.

The concept of The Rebel (1951). Revolt is the movement by which a man says no to a condition he judges unjust and, by this no, affirms a value he holds to be common to all men; its central formula is a cogito, “Je me révolte, donc nous sommes”, I rebel, therefore we are. Camus distinguishes metaphysical revolt, which contests the whole of creation and God himself, from historical revolt, which contests the social order. His book tells how each of them turned into its opposite: revolt, which began by contesting God in the name of man, ends by divinizing man and then history, and by killing in the name of this new divinity. Against this drift, Camus sets measure, the thought of noon, and refuses to let the we of revolt become an absolute. The essay finds in it the unbeliever's answer to the sigh without a heaven: the lament of the oppressed creature changes its address and turns towards other men, on condition that this we remains horizontal, never becomes a god and never designates a victim. See also The absurd, Thought of noon, Divinization of history, Sigh without a heaven.

The last part of The Rebel (1951), and the name Camus gives to a thought of limits. Against the revolts that turned into religions of history, he appeals to the Mediterranean, to Greek light, to the measure that knows that every value affirmed against injustice destroys itself if it becomes absolute. The sentence that condenses it is the one the essay quotes twice: at the noon of thought, the rebel refuses divinity in order to share the common struggles and destiny. The essay makes of it the measure expressly directed against the divinization of history, and notes that Camus's noon answers Nietzsche's noon, the hour when there is no longer any world behind the world; Nietzschean spirituality, which is not a replacement religion, becomes in Camus the thought of noon. It formulates a reservation: Camus's Mediterranean is an aesthetic myth, the most discreet form of refoundation, which is nonetheless not enough to place him among the refounders, and it is as an exception of attitude, unstable like Nietzsche, that Camus figures in the conclusion. See also Revolt, Divinization of history, Amor fati.

The expression of The Rebel by which Camus describes the outcome of modern revolts: cynicism, the divinization of history and of matter, individual terror or state crime. Revolt begins by contesting God in the name of man; it ends by divinizing man, then history, and by killing in the name of this new divinity, the regicides of 1793 and the deicides of the nineteenth century preparing the totalitarianisms of the twentieth. Marxism has not left religion: it has turned revolt into a religion of history, whose meaning, placed in the future, justifies every present sacrifice. The essay writes that the divinization of history is, in Camus, the name of what it itself calls the refoundation of a religion, and it ranks the History of the revolutionaries among the strict refoundations of its conclusion, alongside Plato's city and Comte's Great Being. The quarrel of 1952 with Jeanson and Sartre bore on this chapter; the essay sides with Camus on substance and with Sartre on method. Löwith and Voegelin say the same thing in terms of the secularization of eschatology. See also Revolt, Secularized eschatology, Secular religions.

The central notion of Totality and Infinity (1961). The face of the other is neither an object I perceive nor a phenomenon I constitute: it comes from beyond all representation, it always exceeds the idea one forms of it, and speaks to me before any discourse, to say “Tu ne tueras point”, “Thou shalt not kill”. Levinas takes from Descartes the idea of the infinite and carries it over from God to the face: it is in the relation to the other, not in the proof of God, that the infinite is given. Ethics thus becomes first, before ontology, and ethics is an optics: God comes to mind only in the trace left by the face, in responsibility for the other man. The essay sets this asymmetry against the symmetry of I and Thou in Feuerbach, and follows the attested dialogue with Buber. It hesitates over the verdict: Levinas, who rejects the numinous sacred as a violence and holds monotheism to be an atheism with regard to the mythical gods, does not fall under the criterion, though the author is not quite sure of it; he leans towards a believing exception. See also Idol and icon, Numinous, Negative theology.

In the historical sense, the currents of the second and third centuries that taught a salvation through knowledge, gnôsis, of a God foreign to an evil world created by an inferior demiurge; the Fathers fought them as the first heresy. In the twentieth century the word becomes a polemical category. Eric Voegelin, in The New Science of Politics (1952), makes gnosis the essence of modernity: from Joachim of Fiore to the totalitarian ideologies, the moderns would seek to realize salvation here below, to immanentize the eschaton, and claim certain knowledge of the meaning of history. Blumenberg, without answering Voegelin himself, turns the formula around: modernity is a second victory over gnosis; Kelsen objects that a theory which recognizes gnosis everywhere proves everything. Buber reproaches Jung with a gnosis of another order: the encounter with an external Thou is replaced by knowledge of an inner content. The essay judges Kelsen and Blumenberg right against Voegelin's genealogy, but wrong against the function Aron describes: secular religion in Aron's sense remains indispensable to it. See also Secular religions, Secularized eschatology, Archetypes and individuation.

Eric Voegelin's formula in The New Science of Politics (1952): modern ideologies, on this view, are the attempt to build within history what Christianity expected from its end, the immanentization of the Christian eschaton. The eschaton is, in Christian theology, the final fulfilment that gives meaning to everything that precedes it, the reign of God after the judgement; to immanentize it is to carry it over from the beyond into the earthly future, in the form of the classless society, the thousand-year Reich or indefinite progress. Löwith had shown in Meaning in History (1949) that the philosophy of history is transposed eschatology; Voegelin makes it a pathology, gnosis, and concludes that totalitarianism is the final form of progressive civilization. The essay retains the support these analyses give its thesis, secular religions being the most massive cases of the criterion, but follows Kelsen and Blumenberg against their genealogy: that the History of the revolutionaries demands sacrifice does not prove that it descends from Christian eschatology; it is function, not origin, that counts. See also Secularized eschatology, Gnosis, Secular religions.

Selbstbehauptung. In The Legitimacy of the Modern Age (1966), Hans Blumenberg maintains that modernity owes its legitimacy to no inheritance, Christian or other, but to a self-assertion, and he dates it precisely: it is man's response to the theological absolutism of the late Middle Ages, that of nominalism, which had made God an arbitrary and omnipotent will before which the world no longer offered any guarantee of order. Faced with a hidden and unpredictable God, man had to take charge of himself, to know and master nature in order to find his way in it. Modernity is therefore not a Christianity that has lost its faith, but a response to an internal crisis of Christian theology, and the secularization theorem, which makes progress a transposed eschatology, is a category of historical injustice. The essay holds Blumenberg to be an unexpected ally, whose intellectual hygiene obliges it to restrict its thesis to the sacrifice criterion. Leo Strauss, with no attested dialogue, is wholly opposed to this reading: modernity is for him a break with ancient wisdom, not a legitimate self-assertion. See also Reoccupation, Secularization, Hidden God.

Leo Strauss's thesis in Persecution and the Art of Writing (1952): the philosophers who wrote under threat, Maimonides, Averroes, Spinoza and many others, composed their books on two levels, an exoteric teaching in keeping with the opinion of the city and an esoteric teaching reserved for attentive readers, which can be deciphered in contradictions, silences and repetitions. Strauss finds its source in Maimonides, whose seventh cause of contradiction, in the introduction to the Guide for the Perplexed, describes a writing for two publics. The essay judges this theory fragile in its general use, but takes seriously the suspicion it casts on Spinoza: the apparent piety of the Ethics, the piety that made him a God-intoxicated man in the eyes of the Romantics, would in part be an art of writing. It replies that the intellectual love of God is demonstrated there, not suggested, while acknowledging that the Spinozist exception rests on an indemonstrable decision. The theory extends the Averroist division between the elite and the multitude that the essay follows from Averroes to Renan and to Strauss. See also Double truth, Taʾwīl, Intellectual love of God.

Literally, receiving one's law from another. In The Disenchantment of the World (1985), Marcel Gauchet uses it to define religion itself: not first of all a belief, but a form of society in which the rules of common life are not made by men but given to them by the gods, the ancestors, the time of origins. The stateless societies studied by ethnologists are its purest form, the one in which dispossession is most complete. The history of the great religions is that of a progressive reduction of this heteronomy: an ever more transcendent God leaves the world ever more to men, until democracy becomes the regime of a society that gives itself its own law and must live without an external guarantor, autonomy after heteronomy. It is in this sense that Christianity is the religion of the exit from religion. The essay sees in Gauchet the historian of the exit, not the thinker of what remains, since the exit from religion does not mean the exit from belief. See also Religion of the exit from religion, Disenchantment of the world, Secularization.

fr: Religion de la sortie de la religion
terme: Religion of the exit from religion
motifs: religion of the exit from religion
definition: Marcel Gauchet's formula, in The Disenchantment of the World (1985), for defining Christianity. Through the incarnation, which puts God into history, and through the absolute transcendence of a God who withdraws from the world, Christianity made possible a society that organizes itself without reference to the divine: it produced by itself the conditions of its own effacement, and democratic modernity is its fulfilment, not its negation. The essay points out that the thesis is already formulated, in genealogical terms, in § 27 of the third essay of On the Genealogy of Morality, where Nietzsche describes a Christianity that destroys itself out of fidelity to itself, and it compares Gauchet with Girard, for whom Christianity is at once the exit from sacrificial religion and a religion, the two lines of thought sharing the same weakness, which is to make Christianity the end point of the religious history of humanity. It also draws from it a weapon against Onfray's Décadence: if Gauchet is right, Christianity does not die, it fulfils itself. Gauchet specifies in 1998 that the exit from religion does not mean the exit from religious belief. See also Heteronomy, Disenchantment of the world, Scapegoat mechanism.

The notions by which Charles Taylor, in A Secular Age (2007), describes what modernity has built, and which the essay paraphrases. The immanent frame is the natural, social and moral order that can be understood entirely without transcendence and that holds up by itself. Exclusive humanism is the possibility, widely available for the first time, of a life directed towards human flourishing with nothing beyond it. The nova effect is the multiplication of spiritual positions, believing and unbelieving, that this situation engenders. Against subtraction stories, which present secularization as the unveiling of a human nature rid of religion, Taylor maintains that the world from which God is removed is not a bare nature but a new historical construction, with its ideals and its imaginary, and that belief has become one option among others in it. The essay shares the rejection of subtraction stories, which joins its own rejection of a total exit, but not the conclusion of Taylor, for whom faith remains a living option that the secular age makes more difficult but not less true: Stirner turned around, you have built something else, answer for it. See also Secularization, Post-secular, Living, forced, momentous option.

The central concept of the speech “Glauben und Wissen” (“Faith and Knowledge”), delivered by Jürgen Habermas on 14 October 2001: a secularization that does not annihilate is accomplished in the mode of translation, “Eine Säkularisierung, die nicht vernichtet, vollzieht sich im Modus der Übersetzung”. In a post-secular society, where religions persist and where secular reason knows its limits, religious contents should be neither imposed nor rejected, but translated into a language accessible to all; Habermas gives as an example man created in the image of God (Gn 1, 27), whose idea of createdness says, in the face of genetic engineering, something that secular ethics struggles to say, and he holds Kant to be the first example of a secularizing and saving deconstruction. The essay sees in it a third way between Löwith, for whom modernity inherits religious contents, and Blumenberg, for whom it merely reoccupies places. It marks its limit: Habermas translates only normative contents, and does not say how the individual lives without religion, which is the question of Part Twelve. See also Post-secular, Secularization, Reoccupation.

Ἐπιμέλεια ἑαυτοῦ, epimeleia heautou. In The Hermeneutics of the Subject, his 1982 Collège de France course, Foucault shows that in Antiquity the Delphic precept know thyself was subordinate to a more fundamental precept, the care of the self: one could know the truth only by taking care of oneself, that is, by transforming oneself. This is the sense of the definition of spirituality the essay borrows from him, the search, the practice, the experience through which the subject carries out on itself the transformations necessary to have access to the truth. The Cartesian moment marks the end of this subordination. Hadot, whom Foucault had read and drawn upon, expressed after Foucault's death both his esteem and his disagreement: the culture of the self, the care of the self in which the subject constitutes itself as a work, seemed to him too aesthetic, a new form of dandyism, whereas the ancient exercises aimed at going beyond oneself towards the Whole. The essay notes that Foucault does not say what the true is nor whether it exceeds the subject, and that is why it takes the definition from him and the description from Hadot. See also Spirituality, Cartesian moment, Spiritual exercises.

Foucault's expression in The Hermeneutics of the Subject (lecture of 6 January 1982), which the essay paraphrases, not having found the wording on a reliable page. From Descartes onwards, access to truth comes through knowledge alone: all that is needed is a subject who reasons well and follows a method, and no transformation of his being is required any longer; truth becomes a matter of propositions, and spirituality separates from philosophy. The essay uses this framework to explain why the modern critique of religion has almost always targeted religion as belief, as a set of true or false propositions: it is because, since the Cartesian moment, truth has been a matter of propositions. Spinoza is an exception, the Ethics being a book of geometrical demonstrations whose end is a transformation of life; so is Nietzsche, who constantly asks what truth does to the one who seeks it. The essay itself qualifies the notion, in the Descartes section: the Cartesian moment is not a clean break but a conversion of spirituality into metaphysics. See also Care of the self, Spirituality, Will to truth.

Chiffern. For Karl Jaspers, transcendence is not a supreme being that could be known or denied; it is the Encompassing of all encompassings, and it gives itself only in ciphers: nature, the work of art, the religious symbol, metaphysics itself are ciphers of transcendence, which designate it while withdrawing. What is proper to the cipher is that it refuses knowledge at the very moment it points: it must remain a cipher, and that is why Jaspers reproaches Bultmann, in an attested response of 1954, with translating myths into existential concepts, since myth cannot be translated without loss, and reproaches revelation with turning the cipher into a possessed object. Philosophical faith is the attitude that stands before the ciphers without fixing them into dogmas. The essay ranks Jaspers among the prudent believing exceptions, formulating a reservation about the inflation of ciphers, which ends by saying everything and therefore nothing, and replying to Camus that Jaspers's leap, if it is a philosophical suicide in logic, ends in no obedience. See also Encompassing, Philosophical faith, Limit situations.

Achsenzeit. In The Origin and Goal of History (1949), Karl Jaspers observes that between roughly 800 and 200 BCE, and above all around 500, comparable spiritual events took place independently of one another in China, India, Iran, Palestine and Greece: Confucius and Lao-tzu, the Upanishads and the Buddha, Zarathustra, the prophets of Israel, the Greek philosophers. Everywhere man becomes conscious of himself and of his limits, raises the question of the Whole and calls received myths into doubt. Jaspers makes it the axis of universal history, in place of the Christian axis of the Incarnation, which holds only for Christians. The essay finds in it what gives Jaspers his place in an inquiry that seeks to move beyond Christianity alone: the critique of religion and the spirituality of exercise have multiple sources, and the history the essay tells, centred by avowal on Christian and post-Christian Europe, is only one of the paths. The notion was taken up by sociologists, from Shmuel Eisenstadt to Robert Bellah, and debated for its chronology. See also Philosophical faith, Encompassing, Relay fable.

Disengagement from the self. In The Sovereignty of Good (1970), Iris Murdoch describes the moral life not as a series of choices of the will, against Sartre and the analytic philosophy of her time, but as a work of attention, a word taken from Simone Weil. The enemy is the fat, relentless ego, which covers reality with its fantasies; moral progress consists in silencing it in order to see what is. Murdoch calls this silence unselfing, and gives as its example the kestrel: she glimpses through the window a hovering kestrel, and there is nothing now but kestrel. Her sharpest formula, which the essay quotes, says that we cease to be in order to attend to the existence of something else. The object of this attention is no longer God, a single, perfect, transcendent, non-representable and necessarily real object, but the Good, taken from Plato and the sun of the Republic, which judges the world without blessing it, against Comte-Sponville. The essay sees in it the sober transposition of Weil's decreation and ranks Murdoch among the exceptions, the position of transcendence without God: an absolute that demands nothing but attention. See also Decreation, Periagôgê, Spirituality of exercise.

Nirvāṇa, extinction. In Buddhism, the cessation of the craving, hatred and ignorance that feed the cycle of rebirths, and thereby the end of suffering; the schools debate whether it should be seen as a mere cessation or as an ineffable positive state. The essay first encounters it through Schopenhauer, who makes nirvana the mythical expression of the denial of the will to live and quotes, in § 63 of The World as Will and Representation, the Buddhist promise as he read it: a state in which there is neither birth, nor old age, nor sickness, nor death. It then shows, with Roger-Pol Droit, that the Buddhism of the European philosophers of the nineteenth century, a cult of nothingness for some, a positivist religion without God for Nietzsche, is a projection of Europe, and that real Buddhism is a complete tradition, with gods, karma, the saṅgha and the triple refuge: religion is not defined by God. Buddhism is for the essay neither an exception nor an ally, but a test, and the corporate meditation of the contemporary West is a reinvention of it, described as palliative care. See also Will to live, Nihilism, Spiritual exercises.

André Comte-Sponville's position in L'Esprit de l'athéisme (2006). He has lost faith, not fidelity to what the Christian tradition taught him of justice, compassion and love: the best that religion brought, the bond between human beings, attachment to transmitted values, can survive faith. Atheism is for him a belief, not knowledge, and he defends a spirituality without God, founded on the oceanic experience that Rolland set against Freud: the Kingdom is here and now; everything is immanent to the Whole; a God, what for? The universe is enough. The essay situates him between Spinoza, towards whose position of immanence he tends, and Freud, whose atheism he holds to, and reports, according to a formula it has not been able to verify, that Onfray is said to have called him a Christian atheist, that is, a pious atheist in Stirner's sense. Its verdict is twofold: Comte-Sponville refounds nothing, no sacrificial absolute, but his wisdom consoles and does not protest, as Hausemer objects to him regarding the disappearance of evil; he lacks Marx's Protestation, and he does not refound without being an exception. See also Oceanic feeling, Christian atheist, Protestation.

Luc Ferry's notions in L'Homme-Dieu ou le Sens de la vie (1996). Modernity has known a double movement, the humanization of the divine, by which Christianity became ethics and feeling, and the divinization of the human, by which man became the object of sacred values: one no longer dies for God, but for freedom, for human rights, and it does happen. Ferry calls this structure a transcendence within immanence, or horizontal transcendence: the sacred is no longer above, in heaven, but in front, in other human beings and in the horizon of meaning they open. The essay reports the objections of Agnès Antoine and Serge Cantin, who ask whether a transcendence lodged within the immanence of consciousness still deserves the name, and concludes that this is a soft refoundation: Ferry consecrates without demanding, nothing in his work asks anyone to die, but he calls these devotions sacred, and that is the need to consecrate for which Engels reproached Feuerbach. It is the most liberal form of refoundation, opposed to Comte-Sponville's acceptance without transcendence. See also Strict refoundation and soft refoundation, Homo homini Deus, Religion of Humanity.

The notions of Mohammed Arkoun, whom the essay knows at second hand, through Tauil and Demorgon, with the reservation it states itself. Arkoun describes, in Pour une critique de la raison islamique (1984), the process by which an orthodoxy constituted itself in Islam after the debates of the first centuries, those of the Mu'tazilites and the philosophers: the dogmatic closure, of which the profession of faith of al-Qadir in the eleventh century is a milestone, sets limits not to be crossed, and a whole unthinkable takes shape. The unthought is what has not yet been thought; the unthinkable, what an orthodoxy has made impossible to think, and the discontinuities of Islamic history, the lost debates, the abandoned possibilities, vanish into this sphere. The essay notes that this vocabulary comes from the French thought of Arkoun's time, and situates the project: Arkoun leaves the closure, not religion, on the side of Spinoza and Ricoeur, by reopening Islam to its history. It ranks al-Qadir's dogmatic closure among the strict refoundations and concludes that the exit from religion is first of all Christian, but not only Christian. See also Double truth, Taʾwīl, Second naïveté.

The expression by which Michel Onfray, according to a reported formula the essay has not been able to verify, is said to have described André Comte-Sponville, and which he turns into a category, Christian atheism, in the Traité d'athéologie (2005): the atheist who keeps Christian morality, compassion, humility, love of one's neighbour, abandoning only God, is still a pious atheist in Stirner's sense. The essay notes that Spanish criticism has applied the same expression to Onfray, atheology as the discourse of Christian atheism, and that the irony became complete in 2021, when Onfray defended the Latin Mass as liturgical heritage and declared that his world is the one the God of the Christians made possible. Onfray has in turn become a Christian atheist, but differently: Comte-Sponville keeps from Christianity an inner fidelity, a spirituality without a Church; Onfray keeps from it an outward civilization, a Church without spirituality. According to the criterion, the first refounds nothing and the second refounds a collective absolute, Civilization, a contemporary case of Stirner's law and of the figure of the Grand Inquisitor. See also Faithful atheist, Pious atheists, Atheology.

The pair that structures Part Twelve and the quarrel of the two wisdoms. Transcendent is what goes beyond the world or the subject and remains external to it, the creator God, Plato's Good, Plotinus's One; immanent is what remains within the world and has no principle other than it, God or Nature in Spinoza, Comte-Sponville's Whole, Taylor's immanent frame. The essay refuses to make this pair the criterion of the exit from religion: thoughts of transcendence, Murdoch, Weil, Levinas, install no absolute that demands, and thoughts of immanence, the cult of Humanity or of History, do install one. It makes it rather the axis along which the exceptions are classified: the position of immanence, Spinoza and Hadot, towards which Comte-Sponville tends; transcendence without God, Murdoch; the silent version, Wittgenstein. The quarrel between Comte-Sponville and Ferry sets acceptance without transcendence against transcendence without God, the first closer to an exit, the second better able to hear Marx's Protestation, and the conclusion attempts to hold both. See also Deus seu Natura, Man-God and horizontal transcendence, Sacrifice criterion.

In the Bible, the pact by which God binds himself to a people or to humanity and expects fidelity from it. The narratives give several: with Noah and every living creature, sealed by the bow in the cloud; with Abraham, marked by circumcision; at Sinai with Israel, of which the Decalogue and the Law are the terms; with David, to whom a royal line is promised. Jeremiah announces a new covenant, written on hearts; Christians take up the formula at the Last Supper and call their own Scriptures the New Testament, that is, the new covenant, which makes the Jewish Bible an Old Testament. The essay holds with Sanders that the Judaism of Paul's time was already a religion of the covenant received by grace, not a religion of works, and that Paul does not leave it for another. See also Torah, Messiah.

The anointed one, the one consecrated by anointing: the king of Israel, sometimes the priest. After the end of the monarchy, the word designates the descendant of David awaited to restore the people and justice, a varied figure in the time of Jesus, king, priest or heavenly envoy. The Greek Christos translates it, and Christians make it the title, then almost the name, of Jesus, executed by Rome as king of the Jews. Rabbinic Judaism keeps the expectation of a messiah to come. The essay meets the word in Reimarus, for whom Jesus was a political Jewish messiah who failed, in Strauss, for whom a community awaiting a Messiah gives Jesus the features the Scriptures attributed to him, and in Löwith, who reads the philosophies of history as a transposed messianism. See also eschatology, Covenant.

The list of books a community recognizes as Scripture. The Greek word designates the mason's rule, then the norm and the catalogue. The Jewish canon, fixed gradually, counts twenty-four books; the Christian canon of the Old Testament varies between confessions, Catholics and Orthodox receiving Greek books that Protestants set aside. The twenty-seven books of the New Testament imposed themselves through liturgical use over roughly two centuries, before being recorded in lists, among them the festal letter of Athanasius in 367, then defined by the Council of Trent in 1546. The criteria invoked, apostolic origin, conformity to the faith, wide reception, antiquity, serve above all to justify an established usage. For a text, being outside the canon means not being read in the assembly, not being without historical value. See also Apocrypha.

Literally hidden. The word first designates books reserved for initiates, then books that are not read in the assembly and whose origin is judged doubtful. Its meaning varies between confessions: Protestants call apocrypha the Greek books of the Old Testament, Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Maccabees, which Catholics call deuterocanonical and receive; all call apocryphal the gospels, acts and apocalypses excluded from the New Testament, such as the Gospel of Thomas or the Protevangelium of James. A pseudepigraphon is a writing placed under the name of an ancient figure, Enoch or an apostle, a common practice in Antiquity. The apocrypha tell us little about Jesus, but much about the diversity of Christians in the second century and about the origin of popular traditions, from the manger to the parents of Mary. See also Biblical canon.

The teaching or the Law: in the narrow sense, the first five books of the Bible, from Genesis to Deuteronomy, which the Greeks called the Pentateuch and which tradition attributes to Moses; in the broad sense, the whole of revealed teaching, written and oral. Rabbinic Judaism holds that the oral Torah, set down in writing in the Mishnah and then the Talmud, was given at Sinai together with the written Torah. It contains narratives and commandments, six hundred and thirteen by the rabbinic count, among them the rules of the Sabbath, of purity and of sacrifices. The Greek translation by nomos, law, steered the Christian reading, above all in Paul, towards an opposition between the Law and grace that recent scholarship qualifies. The essay follows in Maimonides, author of the Mishneh Torah, the effort to give a reason for the commandments, and in Levinas the formula to love the Torah more than God. See also Covenant.

In Carl Schmitt (*Politische Theologie*, 1922), the thesis that all the significant concepts of the modern theory of the state are secularized theological concepts: the sovereign who decides on the exception is the omnipotent God become lawgiver, the state of exception corresponds to the miracle, deism to the constitutional state that excludes the sovereign's intervention. Schmitt does not denounce this filiation, he claims it, with Donoso Cortés against liberalism, and the essay ranks him, with Rousseau and Comte, among those who embrace refoundation; in 1933 he would write that the Führer protects the law. Blumenberg replies that these concepts are theologized rather than secularized (attested response, correspondence from 1971 to 1978). Since Varro and Augustine, the expression has also designated the civil theology of cities, and in Spinoza the *Theological-Political Treatise*. The essay sees in it a limit case of refoundation, in the sole form of authority, which it classes among the strict refoundations. See also secularization.
